title: St Mary's Old Church, Clophill – 1963 'Black Mass' desecration
desc: In March 1963 human bones taken from a disturbed 18th-century grave were found arranged inside the ruined church in a pattern the press linked to a Black Mass, along with cockerel feathers and red-painted crosses. Graves were reportedly disturbed again over the following weeks. Students later admitted killing a cockerel there in 1961 as a joke, and the 'sacrifice' idea may owe something to Dennis Wheatley's fiction.

sources.name: Wikipedia – St Mary's Church, Clophill
Historic England – Heritage Calling: 5 chilling tales from churches
Mysterious Britain – Clophill

title: Bluebell Wood, Caddington – animal heads linked to Clophill
desc: On 9 April 1963 the heads of six cows and a horse were found in Bluebell Wood near Caddington. At the height of the Clophill scare, the press linked the find to the supposed black-magic activity at St Mary's. No ritual connection was ever proven. Coordinates are for the village; the wood's exact spot is unconfirmed.

sources.name: Wikipedia – St Mary's Church, Clophill

title: Castle Rising Castle – effigies and sheep's heart
place: Castle Rising, near King's Lynn, Norfolk
desc: On 13 September 1963 a workman reportedly found male and female effigies nailed to the castle door, with a blackened sheep's heart pinned between them with hawthorn twigs and occult symbols drawn on the ground nearby. It was the first of three linked finds in the area. No one was ever identified.

sources.name: Dangerous Minds – The black magic rituals that plagued rural England in 1963

title: Bawsey ruined church – heart, black circle and candle
desc: About four months after the Castle Rising find, a soot-blackened sheep's heart was found nailed to the wall of the ruined Bawsey church with hawthorn twigs. Beside it was a black circle with a black wax candle in the middle. It was reported as part of the same series of ritual finds.

sources.name: Dangerous Minds – The black magic rituals that plagued rural England in 1963

title: Babingley ruined church – ritual objects gathered in tower
desc: In February 1964 a boy fishing nearby reportedly found all three sets of ritual objects from Castle Rising and Bawsey collected inside the bell tower of the ruined Babingley church. The culprit was never identified.

sources.name: Dangerous Minds – The black magic rituals that plagued rural England in 1963

title: St James's ruined church, Bix Bottom
desc: The roofless Norman church in a Chiltern valley is said to have drawn witchcraft and modern-pagan devotees from about 1925, becoming a pilgrimage spot with reputed ley-line and UFO connections. Its sinister reputation grew after it appeared in the occult films The Witches (1966) and The Blood on Satan's Claw (1971). No dated ritual incident is confirmed in these sources.

sources.name: Dark Oxfordshire – The ruins of St James's church, Bix Bottom
Historic England – Ruins of Church of St James

title: Highgate Cemetery – 'Highgate Vampire' and black-magic claims
desc: From 1969–70 a media frenzy over an alleged vampire brought crowds of night-time 'hunters' into the cemetery, and vaults were broken into. In August 1970 charred, headless remains were found near the catacombs, and police reportedly suspected black magic. A 1974 conviction for damaging memorials and interfering with remains followed. Much of the story is seen as press embellishment fuelled by a rivalry between two occultists.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Highgate Vampire
Mental Floss – The bizarre 1970 vampire panic of Highgate Cemetery

title: Tottenham Park Cemetery – Halloween 1968 grave desecration
desc: On Halloween 1968 graves were desecrated by a group said to be interested in the occult. The London Evening News reported flowers laid in circles and a coffin opened, with an iron stake driven into the corpse. The culprits were never identified, but the case was later tied to the Highgate Vampire story.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Highgate Vampire

title: Hellfire Caves, West Wycombe
desc: Chalk caves were dug for Sir Francis Dashwood from 1748 to 1752, and his club, later known as the Hellfire Club, met there in the 1750s and early 1760s. Rumour cast members as devil-worshippers holding mock religious rites and orgies. Contemporary sources describe their practice more as pagan revelry dedicated to Bacchus and Venus. The innermost chamber, beyond an underground 'River Styx', lies beneath St Lawrence's Church.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Hellfire Caves

title: Medmenham Abbey – the 'Monks of Medmenham'
desc: Before the caves, Dashwood's club met at the remodelled Medmenham Abbey on the Thames as the 'Monks of Medmenham'. It was accused of holding obscene parodies of religious rites. The club was in disrepute by 1762 and had largely broken up by 1763.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Medmenham Abbey

title: Montpelier Hill – Dublin Hellfire Club lodge
desc: The ruined hunting lodge on the hill was linked to the 18th-century Irish Hellfire Club. Legends tell of black masses, a chair kept empty for the Devil, black-cat sacrifices and a cloven-hoofed card player. Little of this can be verified, and the stories are best treated as folklore. The lodge itself was built over an ancient cairn.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Montpelier Hill
Dublin.ie – The Hell Fire Club
Irish Post – The Hellfire Club: seven facts

title: Boleskine House – Crowley's Abramelin working
desc: Aleister Crowley bought the house in 1899 to carry out the Abramelin operation, a months-long ritual meant to contact one's Holy Guardian Angel that also involves summoning and binding demonic princes. Legend says he broke off the working without banishing the spirits. The house was later owned by Jimmy Page and was badly damaged by fires in 2015 and 2019.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Boleskine House
The Scotsman – Historic Loch Ness home used for black magic rituals

title: Netherwood, The Ridge – Crowley's last home
desc: Crowley spent his final years in Room 13 of the Netherwood boarding house on The Ridge and died there on 1 December 1947, still writing and designing his Thoth Tarot. Hastings council reportedly refused to let him be cremated in the town. Coordinates are approximate for The Ridge.

sources.name: Hastings Independent Press – The Beast of Hastings

title: Brighton crematorium – Crowley's 'Last Ritual'
desc: Crowley was cremated in Brighton on 5 December 1947 without a religious service. Instead, about 20 mourners heard readings from his magical works, including the 'Hymn to Pan', the Gnostic Mass and The Book of the Law. The press reported it as a pagan or black-magic rite. The source names only the town, so the pin uses approximate coordinates for Woodvale Crematorium.

sources.name: Aleister Crowley Timeline – Daily Herald, 6 Dec 1947
Aleister Crowley Timeline – The Last Ritual

title: Chanctonbury Ring – Devil-summoning hilltop
desc: Legend says the Devil can be summoned by running seven times anticlockwise around the hill-fort's tree ring, and he will offer soup or porridge in exchange for your soul. Crowley and Victor Neuburg, who lived in nearby Steyning, reportedly regarded the Ring as a 'place of power'. The earliest printed version of the summoning legend dates only from 1909.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Chanctonbury Ring
Mysterious Britain – Chanctonbury Ring

title: Rollright Stones – witches' coven lore and modern rites
desc: Local tradition tells of a witch who turned a king and his men to stone. Later accounts say a coven held 'heathen ceremonies' at the circle in Victorian times. In the 20th century the stones became important to figures in modern witchcraft, and an occultist devised a long ritual for the circle that people are said still to perform. Ribbons and clooties are still tied to the tree there.

sources.name: Mysteries of Mercia – The Rollright Stones
World History Encyclopedia – Legends of the Rollright Stones

title: Castle Ring, Cannock Chase – sacrifice legends
desc: The Iron Age hill fort at the highest point of Cannock Chase is locally 'supposed' to have been the site of satanic rituals and human sacrifice by the Cornovii tribe. The claim is unsourced folklore. The Chase is better known for black-eyed-child, pig-man and werewolf reports.

sources.name: Express & Star – If you go down to the Chase today
Wikipedia – Castle Ring

title: Malkin Tower Farm, Blacko – Pendle witches' Good Friday meeting
desc: On Good Friday 1612 friends of the Demdike family allegedly met at Malkin Tower, which magistrate Roger Nowell decided was a witches' coven. The meeting led to the Pendle witch trials, in which most of the accused were hanged. The tower's true site is unknown, and Malkin Tower Farm at Blacko is one of three candidates.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Malkin Tower
Archaeology Magazine – Searching for the Witches' Tower

title: 'Witch's cottage' with mummified cat, Lower Black Moss
desc: In December 2011 United Utilities workers uncovered a buried 17th-century cottage near Lower Black Moss reservoir. A mummified cat was found bricked into the wall of a sealed room, which was taken as a counter-witchcraft charm. Some suggested it was Malkin Tower, but historians dispute this. Coordinates are approximate for the reservoir.

sources.name: Mysterious Britain – Witch's Cottage, Barley
Wikipedia – Malkin Tower
Burnley Express – 'Witches' cottage with mummified cat

title: Lancaster Castle – Pendle witch trials
desc: The Pendle accused were held in Lancaster Gaol and tried at the Lancaster Assizes in August 1612. Their alleged Good Friday plot was supposedly to free prisoners by blowing up the castle. Most were convicted and hanged nearby.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Malkin Tower

title: St Leonard's churchyard, Walton-le-Dale – necromancy legend
desc: According to John Weever's 1631 account, Edward Kelley and a companion (in some versions Dr John Dee too) exhumed a newly buried corpse here at midnight around 1560. They supposedly used a wand, a consecrated torch and incantations to make it reveal hidden treasure. Later folklore adds a vicar who summoned the Devil in green smoke. All of this is legend.

sources.name: Spooky Isles – Lancashire graveyards

title: Meon Hill – 1945 'witchcraft murder'
desc: An elderly farm labourer was found killed on the slopes of Meon Hill on St Valentine's Day 1945. Locals believed he was a witch, and Scotland Yard's detective later called the killing the climax of a pagan rite to enrich the soil with blood. Gerald Gardner disputed that interpretation. The case remains unsolved.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Killing on Meon Hill (Lower Quinton)
Spooky Isles – The Lower Quinton Witchcraft Murder

title: Hagley Wood – 'Bella in the Wych Elm'
desc: Boys found a woman's skull inside a hollow wych elm in Hagley Wood in 1943. In 1945 anthropologist Margaret Murray suggested she had been killed in an occult rite to make a 'Hand of Glory', because one hand had been severed. Graffiti asking 'Who put Bella in the wych elm?' appeared locally. The woman has never been identified and the case is unsolved.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Who put Bella in the wych elm?
Mysterious Britain – Who Put Bella in the Wych Elm?

title: The Sands woods – 'working magic circle'
desc: On 2 August 1990 schoolchildren found a ritual enclosure in woods near The Sands, about 30 paces across and walled with branches. It had a wooden throne, a central hearth and a carved Asherah pole. Police described it as a working magic circle used for sex rites.

sources.name: Liphook Herald – Peeps into the past: sex circle in The Sands

title: St Peter's Church, Bramshaw – satanic graffiti amid livestock attacks
desc: In November 2019 an inverted cross, '666' and other satanic and phallic symbols were painted on the door of this Grade II* listed church. It happened during a spate of nearby livestock attacks, including sheep slashed and marked with pentagrams at Bramshaw.

sources.name: Church Times – Church daubed with satanic symbols near site of attacks on livestock

title: Stagbury Hill trig point – five animal hearts and candles
place: Stagbury Hill, near Bramshaw, New Forest
desc: On 13 January 2023 a hiker found five animal hearts laid out in a pattern on top of the triangulation pillar, ringed by candles. Hampshire police were informed. It followed earlier occult-style incidents around Bramshaw. Coordinates are approximate.

sources.name: CBN News – UK church targeted in gruesome ritual
Christian Post – Witchcraft suspected after 5 animal hearts found

title: Burley centenary stone – deer head and inverted cross
desc: On 8 May 2024 a rotting deer's head and an upside-down cross were left on the centenary stone or milestone by Burley High Street. Police treated it as the latest in a series of 'occult' incidents in the New Forest.

sources.name: ITV Meridian – Severed deer head placed on New Forest memorial stone

title: Hopwas Wood – 1984 ritual and occult artefacts
desc: In 1984 police were called to reports of naked 'witches' dancing in the wood and found a burnt-out fire, small bird bones and a pentagram scratched in the ground. The group said they belonged to a Crowleyan order and were charged only with cannabis possession. In 2010 an Egyptian-style figurine and an engraved Enochian copper tablet were found in the wood.

sources.name: Bad Witch blog – Controversy over witches of Hopwas Wood (citing Tamworth Herald)

title: Vixen Tor – sheep arranged in a heptagram
desc: In January 2005 seven sheep with broken necks were found near Vixen Tor arranged in a seven-pointed star. In October six more were found nearby at Moortown with their eyes removed, laid near a group of stones. Police linked the incidents to a supposed ancient pagan altar east of the tor.

sources.name: The Modern Antiquarian – Terror on the Tor (news)

title: Knocksink Woods – dog sacrificed on stone altar
desc: In summer 2006 hikers found a border collie killed and laid on a cement-and-stone altar inside a ring of stones, some carved with crosses, well away from the marked trails. Gardaí investigated it as a ritual killing and the altar was broken up.

sources.name: Irish Examiner – Gardaí probe ritual sacrifice of dog in remote woods

title: Moville church – '666' altar desecration
desc: In early August 2016 intruders wrote '666' on altar cloths and drew satanic symbols (triangles inside circles) in churches across Inishowen, including at Moville. Gardaí from Carndonagh investigated.

sources.name: Irish Examiner – Churches targeted in apparent acts of 'devil worship'

title: Malin church – '666' altar desecration
desc: Malin was one of three Inishowen churches entered in early August 2016. Intruders marked the altar cloths with '666' and drew occult triangle-in-circle symbols.

sources.name: Irish Examiner – Churches targeted in apparent acts of 'devil worship'

title: Culdaff church – '666' altar desecration
desc: Culdaff was the third church hit in the August 2016 Inishowen 'devil worship' incidents. As at the others, '666' and satanic symbols were left on the altar cloths.

sources.name: Irish Examiner – Churches targeted in apparent acts of 'devil worship'

title: Kyteler's House, Kilkenny – Ireland's first witchcraft trial
desc: In 1324 the Bishop of Ossory accused Dame Alice Kyteler of sorcery, including sacrificing animals to a demon at crossroads and brewing potions in a skull. She fled abroad, and her servant was burned at the stake. Her house survives as Kyteler's Inn.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Alice Kyteler
History Ireland – The Sorcery Trial of Alice Kyteler

title: St Andrew's Auld Kirk, North Berwick – 1590 witches' sabbat
desc: Accused people in the North Berwick trials confessed under torture to meeting the Devil in the Auld Kirk at night on Halloween 1590. One claimed some 200 witches had gathered there to raise storms against James VI. The kirk ruins stand by the harbour.

sources.name: Wikipedia – North Berwick witch trials
Survey of Scottish Witchcraft

title: Witches' Mill, Castletown – Gardner's museum and coven
place: Arbory Street, Castletown, Isle of Man
desc: The old mill housed a museum of witchcraft in the 1950s and 60s, run by Gerald Gardner, the founder of Wicca. Local stories recall residents who were alarmed to share the town with a witch and his small coven. Coordinates are approximate.

sources.name: Island Escapes – A folklore walk around Castletown
Bad Witch blog – Gerald Gardner and witchcraft on the Isle of Man

title: Slieau Whallian – witches' spiked-barrel hill
desc: Manx tradition says people accused of witchcraft were rolled down this hill above St John's in barrels lined with inward-pointing spikes. In one tale the 'Witch of Slieau Whallian' survived and was later burned in Castletown. This is folklore rather than a documented event.

sources.name: IOM Today – The macabre hill with lush woodland
Island Escapes – A folklore walk around Castletown

title: St Beuno's Church, Pistyll – 1991 blood ritual
desc: In September 1991 a warden found what looked like the remains of a black-magic ceremony: blood sprinkled around the altar and floor, and feathers stuck to the steps. Caravanners nearby had seen lights in the unlit church at about 2am. The church began locking its doors afterwards.

sources.name: Daily Post – Memory Lane: blood-drinking black magic

title: St Mary's Church, Conwy – occult graffiti
desc: In March 1987 occult symbols were scrawled on gravestones and church doors at St Mary's. It was one of a run of North Wales church incidents in the late 1980s that the press linked to a local coven.

sources.name: Daily Post – Creepy Conwy witchcraft
Daily Post – North Wales X Files: dark side of witchcraft

title: St Benedict's Church, Gyffin – occult graffiti
desc: In the same month as the Conwy incident, March 1987, similar occult symbols were scrawled at St Benedict's in Gyffin.

sources.name: Daily Post – Creepy Conwy witchcraft

title: Holy Trinity Church, Llandudno – altar desecrated for 'occult rituals'
desc: In June 1987 two teenagers desecrated the altar. One told police he was a pagan and had stolen church ornaments for use in occult rituals, and the pair appeared before the juvenile court.

sources.name: Daily Post – Creepy Conwy witchcraft
Bad Witch blog – News story on dark side of witchcraft

title: St Hilary's Church, Llanrhos – inverted gravestone crosses
desc: In the late 1980s crosses on gravestones in St Hilary's churchyard were turned upside down and other stones were smashed. The vicar publicly suspected a coven at work.

sources.name: Daily Post – North Wales X Files: dark side of witchcraft
Daily Post – Creepy Conwy witchcraft

title: Bryn-y-Maen parish church – inverted cross and occult slogans
desc: In October 1991 a cross was found turned upside down and occult slogans were daubed in the parish registers. The church was closed to the public afterwards.

sources.name: Daily Post – Creepy Conwy witchcraft
Daily Post – North Wales X Files: dark side of witchcraft

title: Ffynnon Elian – the cursing well
desc: Once one of the most famous holy wells in Wales, St Elian's well became notorious in the 18th and 19th centuries as a cursing well. A well-keeper would 'enter' a victim's name, written on a slate or a pin, into the water for a fee. It was feared across North Wales until it was destroyed in the 19th century. Coordinates are approximate.

sources.name: Wellhopper – Ffynnon Elian, Llanelian-yn-Rhos
British Pilgrimage Trust – St Elian's church and a cursing well
Mysterious Britain – Ffynnon Elian

title: Denbigh town square – first Welsh witch execution
desc: In 1594 Gwen ferch Ellis, a healer from Llandyrnog who had lived at Llanelian-yn-Rhos and Betws yn Rhos, was convicted of witchcraft after a charm written backwards was found at the home of the gentleman Thomas Mostyn. She was hanged in Denbigh's town square, the first person executed for witchcraft in Wales.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Gwen ferch Ellis
Dictionary of Welsh Biography – Gwen ferch Ellis
Aberystwyth University – first Welshwoman executed for witchcraft

title: Caernarfon Great Sessions – Llannor witch hangings
desc: In 1622 three siblings from Llannor on the Llŷn peninsula were accused of causing a death by witchcraft. They were tried at Caernarfon and hanged, one of the few Welsh witchcraft cases to end in execution.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Witchcraft in early modern Wales

title: Beaumaris – 1655 witch hanging
desc: In 1655 a woman was accused of cursing another woman who then died. She was tried at Beaumaris and hanged.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Witchcraft in early modern Wales

title: Llanddona – the witches of Llanddona
desc: Anglesey folklore says Llanddona was home to a family of witches who arrived by sea and whose powers passed from mother to daughter. They were feared for their curses and begging threats. This is legend rather than recorded ritual.

sources.name: Wikipedia – Llanddona
Sacred Texts – Welsh Folk-Lore (Llanddona witches)

title: Thor's Stone, Thurstaston Common – 'Viking altar' legend
desc: Local legend says Norse settlers from nearby Thingwell used this sandstone outcrop as a pagan altar for blood sacrifices to Thor. The Thor connection is widely regarded as a modern (Victorian-era) myth. Morris dancers still perform May Day rites there.

sources.name: The Northern Antiquarian – Thor's Stone, Thurstaston
